overview.title: Moon Knight, decade by decade
overview.lede: Moon Knight was created in 1975 as a one-off antagonist for a werewolf comic — a mercenary in silver hired to catch a monster — and the character has spent fifty years being rebuilt by people who each saw something different in him: a pulp adventurer, a psychiatric case, a 90s action lead, a horror protagonist, a priest. This is the smallest shelf on the site and the one where the versions disagree most violently.

sections.h: A hired man in a werewolf comic
body: Werewolf by Night #32, by Doug Moench and Don Perlin. He is a mercenary paid to capture Jack Russell, he wears white so his victims can see him coming, and he was not meant to come back.

He kept coming back, mostly because the costume is one of the best designs Marvel produced in the 1970s: white in the dark, which is the exact inverse of every other night-operating hero and reads instantly.

The multiple identities — Marc Spector the mercenary, Steven Grant the millionaire, Jake Lockley the cab driver — start as a pulp device borrowed from The Shadow, not as a diagnosis. That reading arrives decades later.
The solo book launches in 1980 with Moench writing and a nineteen-year-old Bill Sienkiewicz drawing, and he arrives as a close, obvious Neal Adams imitator — slick, anatomical, photo-real.

Then over about three years, in public, on a monthly deadline, he turns into one of the most radical stylists American comics has produced. The line breaks up. Figures become gestural and distorted. Backgrounds become abstract fields of ink. By the mid-run he is doing collage, scratchboard and paint in a mainstream Marvel monthly.

This is the single best reason to read this shelf, and it is one of the clearest artist evolutions available anywhere in comics. Put issue #1 next to #25 and it is hard to believe it is the same person.
The book also has a genuinely unusual publishing position: it was one of the first Marvel titles sold direct-market only, which is why it could look like this at all.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1980 — competent Neal Adams pastiche. Right: #25, four years later. Same artist.

makers.b: Watch the backgrounds first — that is where he starts experimenting, because editorial notices figures. Blacks stop being shadow and become texture; then the figures follow. By the end he is abandoning outline altogether in places.

sections.h: Fist of Khonshu, and the 90s action hero
body: The 1985 Fist of Khonshu revival pushes the Egyptian material to the front for the first time — before this, Khonshu is mostly set dressing.

Then Marc Spector: Moon Knight runs sixty issues from 1989, and it is a different genre entirely: Chuck Dixon writes him as a straight-ahead action lead with a supporting cast and a mission, in the register Dixon was using on Punisher and later Robin.

The back half is the decade at full volume, and it is where Stephen Platt arrives — an artist hyped enormously at the time on the strength of extremely dense, extremely angular rendering, and who is now the shelf's clearest example of a 90s art fashion that did not last.

fig.cap: Left: Fist of Khonshu, 1985. Right: the Platt era — every surface rendered, nothing at rest.

sections.h: Huston and Finch: the violent one
body: Charlie Huston is a crime novelist, and his Moon Knight is the most brutal version there has been — a man who is genuinely unwell, hallucinating Khonshu as a rotting corpse that talks to him, and who mutilates people.
David Finch draws it in a heavy, dark, hyper-rendered style that suits the material and is a long way from Sienkiewicz's invention.
It is the version that most explicitly frames the identities as illness rather than tactic, and every later run is arguing with it.

fig.cap: Finch's #1 — the figure in shadow, and the moon behind.

sections.h: Ellis and Shalvey: six issues, six genres
body: Warren Ellis and Declan Shalvey get six issues and use them for six completely self-contained stories — a police procedural, a ghost story, a heist, a stalking, a rescue, a corridor fight — each in a different formal register.

The design decision everyone remembers is the white suit: Shalvey and colourist Jordie Bellaire put him in a crisp white three-piece with a mask, which is somehow more unsettling than any amount of armour, and is now the look most readers picture.
It also solves the character's oldest structural problem. Moon Knight has never sustained a long run well; Ellis's answer is to stop trying, and write single issues.
This is the most-recommended entry point on the shelf and takes about an hour to read.

fig.cap: The Ellis/Shalvey #1 — a white field, a crescent, and two eyes. Almost nothing on it.

sections.h: MacKay: a priest with a clinic
body: Jed MacKay's move is to stop treating the illness as a mystery and give the character a job: he opens the Midnight Mission, a walk-in clinic in Manhattan for people the supernatural has hurt, and works as Khonshu's priest rather than his weapon.
It is the first version that is meaningfully about service, and it is also the funniest and most humane run on the shelf without losing the horror.
Alessandro Cappuccio draws it with an angular, high-contrast, almost woodcut clarity that owes something to Shalvey and nothing to Finch.

sections.h: The two runs this shelf cannot show you
body: Two acclaimed modern runs have no omnibus and so are missing entirely:
Bendis and Maleev (2011), in which Marc's identities manifest as Captain America, Wolverine and Spider-Man — a genuinely strange twelve issues.

And more painfully, Jeff Lemire and Greg Smallwood (2016), which opens with Marc committed to a psychiatric hospital and is very widely regarded as the best Moon Knight run ever published. Smallwood's formal work in it — page layouts that fracture and reassemble as reality does — is extraordinary. It is the single biggest hole on any shelf on this site relative to the size of the shelf.
The notes on From The Dead and the MacKay volume say so on the page.

tone.sub: Seven books and no two of them agree about what this character is.

modes.b: The 1970s and the early solo run — multiple identities as a tactic borrowed from The Shadow, not as a diagnosis. Adventure, not horror.
Sienkiewicz turning into himself in public, monthly, over three years. If you read this shelf for one reason, make it this.
Sixty issues of straight-ahead action, and then Stephen Platt rendering every surface in the book. A period document.
Huston and Finch. A man who is genuinely unwell, a god who looks like a corpse, and consequences that stay on the page.
Ellis and Shalvey: six standalone issues in six registers, and the white suit. An hour to read and the best hour on the shelf.
MacKay's Midnight Mission — a clinic, a congregation, and a character with something to do other than suffer. Funny without losing the horror.

mk-o1.title: Moon Knight Omnibus Vol. 1
mk-o1.lede: From a werewolf comic to his own title, and a nineteen-year-old artist starting a transformation you can watch happen page by page.

body: Werewolf by Night #32 introduces him as a hired man in silver, sent to catch a monster. Doug Moench and Don Perlin built him to be used once.
The costume is why he survived. White, at night — the opposite of every other character operating in the dark — and Moench's stated logic was that he wants to be seen coming.

Bill Sienkiewicz starts on the ongoing at nineteen and starts as an obvious Neal Adams imitator — slick, anatomical, entirely competent and entirely derivative. Marvel hired him partly because he could do that.
Watch the backgrounds. That is where the experimentation begins, and by the end of this volume the shift is already visible.
The identities are still a pulp device at this point — Spector, Grant, Lockley as a way to work three levels of the city. Nobody is calling it an illness yet.

makers.b: Compare a figure from #1 with one from #15. The line weight starts varying — thick where it needs energy, nearly absent elsewhere — which is the first sign of the artist he becomes. Adams never did that.

body: Well regarded, and the near-universal reason given is Sienkiewicz. The Moench scripts are solid 1970s Marvel — competent, a bit wordy, unremarkable — and the art is the event.

Readers who come for the modern psychological version report being surprised how light this is: it is an adventure comic with a good costume, not a horror book. That is worth knowing going in rather than being disappointed by.

mk-o2.title: Moon Knight Omnibus Vol. 2
mk-o2.lede: The end of the original run at Sienkiewicz's peak, the Fist of Khonshu revival, and a long tail of guest appearances.

body: This is where Sienkiewicz arrives. The line has fully broken up, the figures are gestural and sometimes distorted past anatomy, and whole panels are given over to abstract fields of black. He is doing collage and scratchboard in a monthly Marvel comic, and Marvel is letting him because the book is direct-market only and nobody is watching too closely.
He left for New Mutants and then Elektra: Assassin, where the experiment went further still. This volume is the last of him here.

sections.h: Fist of Khonshu, and eleven one-shots
body: The 1985 revival pushes the Egyptian material to the front for the first time, which is where the modern version of the character starts.

The tail of the volume is eleven guest appearances in other people's books, which is why it is chaptered one-per-title rather than as numbered parts. It reads as the period between two eras, because that is what it is.

fig.cap: Left: Sienkiewicz at full stretch. Right: Fist of Khonshu, 1985.

body: The Sienkiewicz issues are the best-regarded material on this shelf and are frequently cited well outside Moon Knight discussion as a landmark of American comics art.
The rest of the volume is much more variable — Fist of Khonshu is short and slight, and eleven guest appearances is a lot of other people's comics. Buy it for the first third.

spector-o1.title: Moon Knight: Marc Spector Omnibus Vol. 1
spector-o1.lede: Sixty issues of straight-ahead action begin. Chuck Dixon writes him as a competent professional with a supporting cast — no illness, no ambiguity.

body: Chuck Dixon was one of the most reliable action writers of the era, and his Moon Knight is exactly that: a mission, a plan, a supporting cast, and a lead who is good at his job.

It is the least psychological version of the character there has been, and it is worth reading precisely for that — it demonstrates that the modern illness-centred reading is a choice rather than an inevitability.
The setting shifts to a base in the Rockies with a support team, which is much closer to a Punisher or Batman structure than to anything in the Moench run.
Liked by the readers who have got to it and rarely discussed. The consistent assessment is well-made, unpretentious action comics — Dixon at his most dependable.

The criticism is that it is generic: strip the costume off and this could be several other Marvel books of the period. Readers who came to Moon Knight for the strangeness find it plain. Note the cover scan on this tile is one of the shelf's low-resolution ones.

spector-o2.title: Moon Knight: Marc Spector Omnibus Vol. 2
spector-o2.lede: The back half, and the decade catches up hard — including the shelf's clearest artefact of a 1990s art fashion.

body: Stephen Platt arrives late in the run and was, briefly, one of the most hyped artists in the industry — extremely dense rendering, extreme angularity, every surface textured and nothing at rest. He was signed away to Image almost immediately.
Whether it reads as spectacular or exhausting is entirely a matter of taste, and it is a genuinely useful thing to have on the shelf: this is what the market wanted in 1994, at full strength.
The run is also pulled hard into line-wide crossovers, which is what happened to every Marvel title in this period.
Two four-issue minis follow: Resurrection War (1998) and High Strangeness (1999). The first is the one comic on this shelf marvel.com does not carry at all, so its Read buttons are grey.

The most divided volume on this small shelf. Readers with affection for early-90s art rate the Platt issues highly; readers without it find them close to unreadable, and the crossover material has few defenders anywhere.
What it does well is complete the story — sixty issues of Marc Spector have an ending here. Its value is as a document of what the decade did to a mid-tier title.

huston-o1.title: Moon Knight by Huston, Benson & Hurwitz Omnibus
huston-o1.lede: A crime novelist takes the book and makes it the most violent version there has been — and the first to treat the identities as illness rather than tactic.

body: Charlie Huston came from hardboiled crime fiction and writes Marc Spector as a man in genuine psychiatric collapse: he sees Khonshu as a decomposing corpse that follows him and demands blood, and the book never resolves whether the god is real.
It is also extremely violent — the run opens with a mutilation and does not soften — and it is the version that most directly frames the multiple identities as a diagnosis.
David Finch's art is heavy, dark and hyper-rendered, and it is the correct register for this even if it is a long way from Sienkiewicz.
Mike Benson and then Gregg Hurwitz continue it, and the Hurwitz issues in particular are better than their obscurity suggests.
Well regarded and genuinely consequential: this is where the modern reading of the character starts, and everything since — Ellis, Lemire, MacKay — is in conversation with it.

The recurring criticism is tone. Several readers find the violence gratuitous and the relentlessness wearing over forty-five issues, and the 'dark and gritty' register of 2006 has dated more than the 1980s material has.
Read the Huston issues at minimum. The cover scan here is another of the shelf's soft ones.

ftd-o1.title: Moon Knight: From The Dead Omnibus
ftd-o1.lede: Six issues, six self-contained stories, six different registers, and the white suit. The best hour on this shelf.

body: Moon Knight had never sustained a long run well, and Warren Ellis's answer was to stop trying: six issues, each a complete story, each a different genre exercise. A police procedural. A ghost story. A heist. A one-room fight. Nothing carries over except the character.
The white three-piece suit with a featureless mask is the design everyone now pictures, and it is a Shalvey and Bellaire invention. It is more unsettling than armour because it is calm.
Declan Shalvey's formal work is the other half — issue #5 is a near-wordless corridor fight staged as a single descending sequence, and it is one of the most-reprinted single issues of the decade.
Brian Wood writes the second half of the volume, which is much less discussed and is decent.

makers.b: Look at how he uses white as a value, not as blank paper. The suit is the brightest thing on every page, so the eye goes to it first regardless of composition, and Shalvey then stages the violence around where he wants you already looking.

fig.cap: #1. A white field, a crescent, two eyes.

body: The Ellis and Shalvey six issues are the most recommended Moon Knight comics there are, and readers describe them as a substantial improvement on everything immediately around them. The white-suit design has been kept by nearly every version since, including on screen.
The reservation is length: six issues is the whole event, and the Brian Wood material that fills out the volume is not at the same level.
If you have never read Moon Knight, start here. It takes about an hour.

mackay-o1.title: Moon Knight by Jed MacKay Omnibus
mackay-o1.lede: He opens a walk-in clinic. The first version of this character that is about service rather than suffering, and the funniest book on the shelf.

body: Jed MacKay's premise is disarmingly practical: rather than solve the illness or dramatise it, give the man a job. The Midnight Mission is a walk-in clinic for people the supernatural has hurt, Moon Knight is Khonshu's priest rather than his weapon, and there is a congregation.

It reframes everything. The multiple identities stop being the plot and become context; the therapy sessions that open many issues are played straight; and the book is funny in a way no previous version risked.
Alessandro Cappuccio draws it with hard, angular, high-contrast clarity — closer to a woodcut than to Finch's rendering — and it is a large part of why a book about a clinic still reads as horror.
Getting here means jumping the Bendis and, more painfully, the Lemire and Smallwood run, neither of which has an omnibus.

Strong reception throughout its run and treated as one of the better recent Marvel books. The specific praise is for the Midnight Mission premise — giving the character a function instead of a condition — and for the balance of horror and humour.
The criticism is that it is less formally daring than Ellis's or Lemire's runs, and that the later stretch loses some focus. Cappuccio's art is widely praised.
Read it second, after From The Dead.
